```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)

set.seed(1)
```

## Airbnb

```{r}
data("nyc_airbnb")

nyc_airbnb =
  nyc_airbnb |> 
  mutate(
    stars = review_scores_location / 2
  ) |> 
  rename(
    borough = neighbourhood_group,
    neighborhood = neighbourhood
  ) |> 
  filter(
    borough != "Staten Island"
  ) |> 
  select(price, stars, borough, neighborhood, room_type)
```

Fit a linear regression!

```{r}
fit = lm(price ~ stars + borough, data = nyc_airbnb)
```

Look at what we have

```{r}
fit
summary(fit)
coef(fit)
fitted.values(fit)
resid(fit)

names(fit)
names(summary(fit))
```

most of this output is bad, but sometimes it's okay

let's do better

```{r}
broom::tidy(fit)
```

pulls out the coefficients and SE, p-value, formatted as a data frame

Let's further format it!

```{r}
broom::tidy(fit) |> 
  select(-std.error) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)

broom::glance(fit)
```

Bronx is the current reference category because it's the first in the alphabetical (and we can tell by it not being there in the table)

Change reference category

```{r}
fit = 
  nyc_airbnb |> 
  mutate(borough = fct_infreq(borough)) |> 
  lm(price ~ stars + borough, data = _)

broom::tidy(fit) |> 
  select(-std.error, -statistic) |> 
  mutate(term = str_replace(term, "borough", "Borough: ")) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

## Diagnostics

diagnostics is basically "look at the residuals"

```{r}
modelr::add_residuals(nyc_airbnb, fit)
```

so we can look at residuals

```{r}
nyc_airbnb |> 
  modelr::add_residuals(fit) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = stars, y = resid)) + 
  geom_point()
```

Residual distribution is skewed and not constant skewed! Low residual variance for low stars but very skewed and more spread in 5 stars. 

```{r}
nyc_airbnb |> 
  modelr::add_residuals(fit) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = borough, y = resid)) + 
  geom_violin()
```

Definite skew distributions. There's a lot concentrated near 0 but long tails with Brooklyn and Manhattan.

Do we trust the 95% CI and p-values for coefficients that come out of this linear regression? Probably no. 

## Hypothesis testing

Individual hypothesis testing is easy—just get the p-values here:

```{r}
broom::tidy(fit) |> 
  mutate(term = str_replace(term, "borough", "Borough: ")) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

I still wouldn't trust it because the underlying assumptions regarding residuals is not met. 

Is borough as a categorical variable significant?

Try testing nested models:

```{r}
fit_null = lm(price ~ stars, data = nyc_airbnb)
fit_alt = lm(price ~ stars + borough, data = nyc_airbnb)

anova(fit_null, fit_alt)
```

ANOVA function constructs the F test to compare these two models. F = 255.59 and p-value is really small, so borough matters!

## Nesting data

Nest data first, then fit models to each thing separately. Like stratification!
Try a more complicated modeL:


Now we're doing `stars * borough` which is asking if there's an interaction. Same with `roomt_type * borough`.
```{r}
nyc_airbnb |> 
  lm(price ~ stars * borough + room_type * borough, data = _) |> 
  broom::tidy() |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

What is the effect of shared room vs. entire apartment in Manhattan? It's kind of a hassle to do this right now.
In just Manhattan: 
```{r}
nyc_airbnb |> 
  filter(borough == "Manhattan") |> 
  lm(price ~ stars + room_type, data = _) |> 
  broom::tidy()
```

We want to see it for each borough. We can copy and paste it over and over and change the borough each time...or we can use iteration!

```{r}
nyc_airbnb |> 
  nest(datasets = -borough)
```

Nested the datasets into each borough!!

Create the airbnb lm function+

```{r}
airbnb_lm = function(data) {
  
  lm(price ~ stars + room_type, data = data)
  
}
```


Back to fitting the function here. Map it across the datasets, use the airbnb_lm function and plug the datasets into the function, and fit the linear modles for each of the items in `datasets`!!

```{r}
nyc_airbnb |> 
  nest(datasets = -borough) |> 
  mutate(fits = map(datasets, airbnb_lm),
         results = map(fits, broom::tidy)) |> 
  pull(results)
```

Now we have 4 linear models associated with it, and tidied up the results of each of those lm fits in a column called `results`. Pulling the results out gives us the dataframes for each borough!

We only care about borough and parameter results:

```{r}
nyc_airbnb |> 
  nest(datasets = -borough) |> 
  mutate(fits = map(datasets, airbnb_lm),
         results = map(fits, broom::tidy)) |> 
  select(-datasets, -fits) |> 
  unnest(results) |> 
  select(borough, term, estimate) |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = term,
    values_from = estimate
  )
```

This is easier to read! You can see the effect of stars is strongest in Manhattan and weakest in the Bronx. 

If you wanted to compare effects of stars across boroughs, you can't nest. You would need to do the interaction term `stars * borough` as a test to see if the interaction term is significant.


Tidyverse gives you a way to create an anonymous function. This is shorthand to create this little function `\(data)` which is the same as `airbnb_lm`. 
```{r}
nyc_airbnb |> 
  nest(datasets = -borough) |> 
  mutate(fits = map(datasets, \(data) lm(price ~ stars + room_type, data = data)),
         results = map(fits, broom::tidy)) |> 
  select(-datasets, -fits) |> 
  unnest(results) |> 
  select(borough, term, estimate) |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = term,
    values_from = estimate
  )
```



```{r}
nyc_airbnb |> 
  filter(borough == "Manhattan") |> 
  nest(datasets = -neighborhood)
```

We have 32 neighborhoods!! Each with each dataset with airbnbs
Fit a model for each of them:

```{r}
nyc_airbnb |> 
  filter(borough == "Manhattan") |> 
  nest(datasets = -neighborhood) |> 
  mutate(fits = map(datasets, \(df) lm(price ~ stars + room_type, data = df)),
         results = map(fits, broom::tidy)
  ) |> 
  select(neighborhood, results) |> 
  unnest(results) |> 
  filter(term == "room_typePrivate room") |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = neighborhood, y = estimate)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 80, hjust = 1))
```

We see some `4 x 5` and `3 x 5` before unnesting. Seems like one of the factor levels for room type is dropping in some areas like Civic Center because it doesn't exist. 


## Logistic regression!

import the WP homicide data:

```{r}
baltimore_df = 
  read_csv("data/homicide-data.csv") |> 
  filter(city == "Baltimore") |> 
  mutate(
    resolved = as.numeric(disposition == "Closed by arrest"),
    victim_age = as.numeric(victim_age)
    )
```

Change the reference category for victim_race and then fit the logistic regression:

```{r}
fit_logistic =
  baltimore_df |> 
  mutate(victim_race = fct_infreq(victim_race)) |> 
  glm(resolved ~ victim_age + victim_race, data = _, family = binomial())

fit_logistic |> 
  broom::tidy() |>
  mutate(OR = exp(estimate)) |> 
  select(term, OR, estimate, p.value) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```
